lane: Chat A — Local Field and Seasonal Grasses
scope_note: These 11 exact-name photo-backed research rows provide broad comparison paths, NOT conclusive species determinations. Category gaps preserve unknown traits and avoid speculative exclusion.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: look for loose, often compound panicle branches with long, drooping, usually awnless multi-flowered spikelets and a true inner membranous ligule. The 1999 flora calls the base rhizomatous while the 2015 Hill Country treatment calls it tufted and subrhizomatous; BOTH beginner base choices remain possible. Separate M. mutica by the upper sterile rudiments, glumes and 3–6 mm ligule on an intact specimen.

diagnostic_checks.check: The earlier Flora-derived dossier calls this a rhizomatous perennial, 50–120 cm tall. Hagenbuch & Lemke (2015, p. 54) instead describe a tufted perennial with no rhizomes or stolons, arising from a hard subrhizomatous base. Preserve this source distinction; inspect the base and do not require spreading rhizomes for identification.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: check a large, branching barnyardgrass panicle with spikelets crowded along the side branches, the typically conspicuous raised-base hairs on leaf sheaths, and an ABSENT true ligule. Long lower-lemma awns are common, but some source-described plants have short or no visible awns. Do not infer an awnless identity from broken immature tips; inspect mature floret/awn origin versus E. crus-galli and E. muricata.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: look for a loosely branched or partly contracted narrow panicle bearing small, often clustered spikelets. Its inner ligule is a minute CILIOLATE membrane (about 0.5 mm): from a beginner's close view it can resemble either a little membrane or a hair fringe. Rooted growth-form and awn states are left unknown. A mature spikelet must gape from the enlarged sterile-floret palea before identifying S. hians confidently.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: a small tufted ANNUAL with narrow, sometimes interrupted-looking flowering panicles and a ragged inner membranous ligule. Separate S. interrupta from perennial, mostly awnless S. obtusata/intermedia by checking intact short-awned 2–3-flowered spikelets, the lemma's two apical teeth and dorsal awn insertion. The ID key cannot reliably encode this single short bent lemma awn as a long awn or a three-awn floret, so awn state is UNKNOWN.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: consider long, narrow to compressed panicles and mostly flat, about 3–4 mm blades in a tufted or rhizomatous perennial. Wipff & Weakley (2022) distinguish T. elongata from T. mutica chiefly by longer 12–25 cm panicles, an upper glume with 3–7 veins and a palea about three-quarters the lemma. Current Eric Knight photographs show panicle forms, NOT those required glume or palea measurements; inner ligule remains UNKNOWN. Do not substitute broad old T. mutica labels.

profiles.field_rule: Research trial: pink pappusgrass has a narrow pinkish-to-straw feathery panicle above a tufted perennial base; its true ligule is a short ring of hairs. The apparent feathery plume comes from about a DOZEN unequal lemma awns per floret, NOT three Aristida-style awns and NOT separate Setaria bristles. The existing four-choice awn categories cannot faithfully encode this structure, so awns are UNKNOWN. Count awns on ONE detached lemma and compare P. mucronulatum before confirming the species.
